summary: Discovery focused on per-token economics and hosting mode tradeoffs. Asteria is evaluating a pilot to serve insurance claim summarization and first-touch chat. Key concerns were latency for customer-facing flows, budget cap per month, data residency, and auditability. Discussed batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization, and dedicated vs hosted/private deployment. Agreed to pilot with guarded burn cap, share pricing/workbook and security docs, and a 2-hour kickoff for pilot scoping.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-10-02
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Michael (Redwood SA), Karen (Asteria Head of AI), Jorge (Platform), Maya (Security), Ethan (PM)

Auto-summary (generated): Medium-quality transcript; call type discovery; focus on cost/unit economics and hosting options.

00:00 Alex (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for making time. i'm alex from redwood, i'm the account lead. quick intros - priya is our se, michael's going to chime in on infra.
00:18 Karen (Asteria): hi all, karen here. we own the ai roadmap at asteria, we want to understand where to run inference for a claims summary flow. budget is tight this quarter, 50K USD cap for pilot month, and latency needs to be customer-perceived under 800 ms ideally.
00:35 Priya (Redwood SE): great, thanks karen. quick clarifying q: when you say latency under 800, is that tail p95 for single-turn chat or for multi-turn document summarization?
00:45 Karen: mostly single-turn chat but we also have a background summarization pipeline that ingests entire claim packets; that can be async. main live experience is the chat.
00:55 Jorge (Asteria): our stack: kubernetes cluster in us-east, we push services via helm. right now we call an external hosted llm for prototypes. security requires SOC2 type 2 and key management with our KMS, plus we need audit logs.
01:10 Michael (Redwood): understood. typical levers we'll walk through: per-token pricing with hosted, dedicated GPU pools for predictable throughput, and private VPC/on-prem if you need full data residency. also batching and prefix/KV cache to reduce token compute.
01:32 Alex: and just to flag early — sometimes the delta between hosted and dedicated depends a lot on your request shape: short chat-turns at low qps often favor hosted for OPEX, large high-qps workloads favor reserved/dedicated.
01:45 Maya (Asteria): our compliance lead asked about encryption and KMS integration — can you do customer-managed keys on hosted?
01:52 Priya: yes, we support KMS for private plane deploys and we do integrations on Dedicated as well. hosted with customer-managed keys is more limited today — we can discuss a private control plane option for the pilot. sometimes the wording in our docs gets misread — it's not "privateplane" — apologies, transcription grabbed a wrong token.
02:10 Ethan (Asteria): budget wise, what does per-token look like for a 7B model vs a 70B model? and can batching help materially?
02:20 Priya: short answer: yes, batching helps but depends on latency SLOs. for example, a 7B quantized variant with 8-bit can be ~3x cheaper per token vs a 70B full-fp model. but the 70B will typically have higher latency and without batching your per-call overhead can dominate. we'll send a workbook with scenarios.
02:40 Alex: to ground this — if you expect 500k tokens/day with average prompt+completion of 80 tokens, we can run the numbers for hosted p95 and dedicated reserved node pricing.
03:05 Jorge: our traffic profile is spiky: weekday mornings 9-11 we get bursts. we can't exceed X throughput or we hit SLAs. can dedicated handle burst capacity?
03:20 Michael: Dedicated pools support autoscaling and burst capacity but there are configured limits. you can set reserved capacity plus burst to hosted fallbacks. that's one of the hybrid patterns we recommend if you want cost predictability but also elasticity.
03:42 Karen: curious — what about KV cache for session history, will that reduce tokens burned?
03:50 Priya: yep — KV/prefix caching reduces repeated transformer compute on shared prefixes. for chat where users have a stable system prompt or often identical initial context, caching can save up to 30-60% of token compute depending on reuse. the tricky part is cache hit rate estimation — we asked you to share sample traffic so we can model this.
04:15 Maya: data residency — we must keep certain PII in-region and encryption at rest with our KMS. In private deployments, can we manage keys entirely?
04:30 Priya: in Private (VPC or on-prem) you control the KMS and we only operate the control plane per contract. Audit logs can be shipped to your SIEM. In Dedicated we have integrations where keys can be customer-controlled depending on contract. Hosted standard doesn't give full KMS control.
04:50 Karen: okay that helps. what about quantization and quality regressions, we can't accept big drops in claim-parsing accuracy.
05:02 Priya: we do model evaluation and can provide eval runs on your prompt sets. quantization frequently preserves quality for classification and summarization tasks with little regression if done carefully; we'll run small A/Bs. we also have rollback and canary controls in our console.
05:28 Jorge: can you provide sample latency measurements and a small benchmark script? we want to run it from our region to see network impact.
05:35 Michael: yes, we'll include a benchmark script in the pilot runbook, along with example load profiles. we usually recommend colocating the pilot in the region you expect production traffic to avoid network noise.
05:55 Ethan: walk me through a simple spend cap for pilot — how do we stop runaway tokens?
06:05 Alex: you can set daily token caps and alerting. for pilots we often put a hard budget cap on the account and configure rate limits and quotas per api-key. we'll also instrument cost telemetry at token-level in the console.
06:30 Karen: any gotchas on pricing sheets? hidden per-request fees?
06:36 Alex: primary charges are per-token generation and per-embedding where applicable. for Dedicated there's a fixed reserved capacity fee. network egress is separate if you use Private on cloud infra tied to your cloud account. we'll make line items explicit in the workbook.
06:55 Maya: from security side, we need SOC2 docs and pen-test summary to get the CISO comfortable.
07:00 Alex: noted — we'll share SOC2 type II report, pen test redacted summary, and an architecture whitepaper that shows where logs live and how KMS is integrated.
07:12 Karen: timeline question — we need a pilot roughly two weeks from now to fit Q4 roadmap. is that realistic?
07:20 Priya: two weeks is tight but feasible for a small scoped pilot: we'll need your traffic sample and a small dataset, plus sign-off on the access model. Dedicated provisioning can take longer but hosted/private pilot variants can be faster.
07:40 Jorge: how long does Dedicated provisioning take?
07:44 Michael: typically 2-4 weeks depending on region and GPU availability; we can sometimes reserve hot-standby capacity earlier with commercial terms.
08:00 Alex: i'll recap — action items: we'll send pricing workbook, pilot runbook and benchmarks, and security docs. you (Asteria) will share traffic profile and retention rules. schedule kickoff for a 2-hr scoping workshop next wednesday? does that work?
08:18 Karen: next wed works. could we also see an example of caching numbers applied to our sample?
08:25 Priya: yes — once we get sample logs we will run a cache-hit simulation and show projected token savings.
08:40 Ethan: quick question — if the pilot hits budget cap, do requests fail or throttle?
08:46 Alex: we can either hard-stop at the cap or throttle gracefully with a 429 and fallback model variant, depends on your preference. for customer facing flows you may want graceful degradation and a cheaper model fallback.
09:05 Maya: last security point — we need to know data retention windows and whether logs can be auto-purged.
09:12 Michael: retention windows are configurable. for hosted we retain logs per the contract; for Private you control retention and logs can be exported to your SIEM and auto-purged.
09:30 Karen: great. thanks everyone.
09:36 Alex: thanks — we'll follow up with the docs.

End of call — 52 minutes total.
